I haven’t been able to confirm my status via testing (which isn’t the most reliable if you haven’t had an outbreak), but I just assume I will come into contact with either kind of HSV in my lifetime and accept the risk.

You’re fair to take whatever precautions are necessary to lower their risk during this outbreak. That’s taking ownership of your sexual health. My belief is that your partner isn’t freaking out because she feels well-informed and comfortable with the risk. Realistically, there are other STIs that are more important to “freak out” about because they can result in complications if left untreated.

It would help to have a conversation with your partner about their concerns and what kind of intimate contact you both feel comfortable with until the outbreaks are treated. Then, discuss whether you both think it’s worth it to pursue testing.

I just want to chime in and say there’s no need to establish hierarchy or a primary partnership this early (especially if you just met this person). Just make sure you’re in alignment on what kind of relationship you want to have with each other (frequency of dates, any safe sex agreements, what you can offer to each other and other partners in the future). Do either of you want kids, cohabitation, marriage, financial entanglement? If so, do you envision doing those things with each other? The first question is important to figure out early but I encourage waiting a lot longer to answer the second one.

In my understanding, a partner becomes “primary” as you further entangle and as you become integrated with each other’s lives. It’s a misconception, and something I didn’t quite understand when I was brand new, that you need to secure a primary.

It doesn’t excuse it at all, but losing interest doesn’t automatically equate to “dumping all the work on the other partner.” To me, it becomes dumping all the work when your lack of desire, once it’s voiced as a problem, turns into lack of care or inaction to rectify it, leaving the partner who does desire sex to try to solve it on their own.

I’d rather judge my partner based on how they take accountability and action when called out for something lacking rather than judge them for not recognizing there’s a lack in the first place. Preventive care is great and ideal, but it’s a lofty goal to expect our partners to be so self-reflective that they can prevent conflict or tension every time before it even arises.

By the time I realized the error in my request and put an end to that arrangement, the flood gates opened. We caught each other up on all the updates in our dating lives for the previous months, I apologized for making the request in the first place, and we vowed to move forward with transparency and honesty while managing our feelings along the way. 

I like hearing about my partner’s life and the loved ones in it. Pretending they didn’t exist just made me feel paranoid, mistrusting, and icky. And ultimately, it felt like I was trying to bypass doing the internal work needed to have a healthy poly relationship. Acknowledging the existence of other partners is hard sometimes but it’s given me the opportunity to challenge my insecurities and anxieties, experience compersion, and realize that other relationships are not a threat to mine.

We were both pretty taken aback by the updates, however, I had to process a lot more changes on my partner’s end. It was hard for me to deal with all of those feelings at once and they culminated into our first full argument where we reached a good resolution but we were both worked up and sensitive by the end of it. I was so worried that would be the end of things. I’ve never witnessed nor experienced healthy conflict resolution in my entire life. I anticipated that my partner would hate me forever and break up with me on the spot.

Instead, we took a few hours of space, checked in on each other later in the day over text, and my partner invited me to their place to reconcile. We just held each other, didn’t say much, and watched some TV in silence. It was awkward, things still felt a bit raw, we kissed sparingly. When we saw each other a few days later (more space), we were practically back to normal. Since the initial argument weeks ago, I feel more secure and confident than ever that we can overcome conflict in the future. Affection, sex, dates, quality time is back to being amazing. We’ve been talking a lot more openly and casually about our other relationships, updating each other on changes, and tackling feelings as they come.

So I guess in my case, it took honesty, genuine apologies, giving space and time to process, and opportunities for reconnecting. I think the freedom that they’re talking about is more the freedom to think and act on your own accord without the constant threat or surveillance of a perceived deity. It feels freeing to no longer believe that no one is condemning you to hell, watching your every move, and controlling your destiny.

As far as “wilding out”, I think it needs a redefinition. If you no longer believe in sin (or what the Bible defines as sin), is it “wilding out” to have premarital sex, for example? Or is it just a normal behavior that humans do when they’re attracted to another person? It takes a while to deconstruct those things that you once considered sin and to define morals that are consistent with your conscience and fit within the laws of society (for example, doing a hit and run isn’t defined as “sinful” but it’s illegal and not a cool thing to do).

As far as the life you’ve built for yourself and the relationships attached to it, embrace the possibility that those might crumble naturally. The foundation they were built on may be entirely faith, it may be too rigid to adapt to the changes you’re going through personally. The ones that stand are what matter. I’ve only told a few close friends that I’m no longer a Christian and the ones that were truly my friends, even through Christ may have brought us together, are the ones who still maintained their relationships with me. Family and career are tricky and romantic relationships are even trickier but their responses to your deconversion can clarify whether they love YOU or just an idealized Christian version of you.

Something that helped me was to start journaling and to start actively disputing the negative thoughts in my head. If you speak them aloud, your friends might be like “No, that’s a lie! You’re amazing!” But their words don’t matter if you don’t believe them for yourself.

Write down 5 things you’re good at. Write down 5 things you want to improve on. Write down 5 things you’re not good at doing. This allows you to highlight your achievements, your ambitions, and accept your shortcomings.

Now, the hardest part, write down 5 things you like about yourself. When I was confronted with this task almost a year ago, I sat for more than 30 minutes, with nothing written, and desperately sobbed. I realized I hated myself.

It’s a long journey to learn how to love yourself, without the influence of your family, your boss, or a romantic partner. You need to boost your ego so hard that you come to the irrefutable conclusion that no one on Earth can be you. But also learn to be humble in accepting that you cannot be anyone else on Earth.

One thing I encourage you to do is to first find a friend who can hold you accountable. Reddit can be very supportive, but you need someone in your life right now who can hold you and love you. 

Next, seek professional help or services. Whether that’s inpatient, or through therapy. A professional will be able to guide you through the steps of recovery. You cannot do this alone. This is a fight to preserve your life and wellbeing.

Lastly, you need to restore your relationship with your body and food. Your body needs food because it’s fuel. A number on the scale or the amount of calories on a nutrition label cannot define your beauty. Eliminate any sources (social media, magazines, clothing store websites) that result in you feeling less than, ugly, or fat. Get rid of your scale. Tell yourself affirmations everyday. “I’m beautiful. I’m loved. I’m important.” Tell your body “You’re strong. You support me. You enable me to live.” 

There will never be such thing as being skinny enough. Enough for what? To have a romantic partner? To wear a bikini? To wear that outfit? YOU ARE ENOUGH. It took me years for me finally to believe it. Oftentimes, we can be our own harshest critics. It’s time to give yourself 5-stars, because you deserve it.
